answer_text:
Let

\[
I_n=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta-n\theta)\,d\theta,
\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots
\]

The key is to recognize the integrand as the real part of a Laurent series on the unit circle.

Set

\[
z=e^{-i\theta}.
\]

Then \(|z|=1\) and

\[
\frac1z=e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta.
\]

Hence

\[
z^n e^{1/z}
= e^{-in\theta} e^{e^{i\theta}}
= e^{-in\theta} e^{\cos\theta+i\sin\theta}
= e^{\cos\theta} e^{i(\sin\theta-n\theta)}.
\]

Taking real parts gives

\[
e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta-n\theta)
=
\operatorname{Re}\left(z^n e^{1/z}\right),
\qquad z=e^{-i\theta}.
\]

Now use the Laurent series of \(e^{1/z}\) on the punctured plane:

\[
e^{1/z}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k!}z^{-k}, \qquad z\neq 0.
\]

Multiplying by \(z^n\),

\[
z^n e^{1/z}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k!}z^{n-k}.
\]

Substitute \(z=e^{-i\theta}\):

\[
z^n e^{1/z}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k!}e^{-i(n-k)\theta}.
\]

Taking real parts,

\[
e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta-n\theta)
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k!}\cos((n-k)\theta).
\]

The series converges uniformly on \([0,\pi]\), so we may integrate term by term:

\[
\int_0^\pi e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta-n\theta)\,d\theta
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k!}
\int_0^\pi \cos((n-k)\theta)\,d\theta.
\]

For any nonzero integer \(m\),

\[
\int_0^\pi \cos(m\theta)\,d\theta
=
\left[\frac{\sin(m\theta)}{m}\right]_0^\pi
=0,
\]

while for \(m=0\),

\[
\int_0^\pi 1\,d\theta=\pi.
\]

Here \(m=n-k\). The only term with \(m=0\) is \(k=n\). Therefore

\[
\int_0^\pi e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta-n\theta)\,d\theta
=
\frac{\pi}{n!}.
\]

Dividing by \(\pi\),

\[
I_n=\frac1{n!}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\frac{1}{n!}}
\]
